messages.content: [Amid WSL title drought, is Arsenal's amazing squad depth really a curse?] play Ona Batlle 'feeling no pressure' replacing Katie McCabe at Arsenal (1:34) For those who are counting, Arsenal have not won a Women's Super League title in seven years. It has been five years since they were even true challengers. This season, though, feels different. This campaign has been designed to change everything: The summer window saw seven new arrivals, there is a renewed strength in depth, and manager Renée Slegers' style of play has been embedded even more. This Arsenal crop is not without any success; they won the 2024-25 Women's Champions League title which, while historic, simultaneously highlighted just how far they had fallen short domestically. European success proved what this group was capable of, but it also raised the question of whether they could translate that level of performance into a sustained WSL title challenge. Slegers inherited a squad largely built for former boss Jonas Eidevall and has spent the last year putting her own stamp on it. This summer, that process accelerated, with Arsenal bringing in goalkeeper Misa Rodríguez , center back Élisa De Almeida , fullback Ona Batlle , midfielders Georgia Stanway and Géraldine Reuteler , and attackers Selina Cerci and Lisa Baum , alongside Isabella Damm . Those arrivals have helped reshape a squad that has also seen the departure of long-serving figures such as forward Beth Mead and defender Katie McCabe , as well as midfielder Victoria Pelova , center back Laia Codina and goalkeeper Manuela Zinsberger . In their place is a group with greater depth, experience and international pedigree, a squad that, on paper, has the quality to challenge for every available trophy. But that depth could ultimately present Slegers with her biggest challenge. For years, squad depth in the WSL has been a problem for most clubs rather than a luxury. messages.content: [Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle] Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba – The Movie: Infinity Castle is a 2025 Japanese animated epic dark fantasy action film based on the "Infinity Castle" arc of the 2016–20 manga series Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba by Koyoharu Gotouge. It is a direct sequel to the fourth season of the anime television series as well as the manga fourth, fifth, and sixth adaptations, following the film Mugen Train (2020) and the feature-length compilations To the Swordsmith Village (2023) and To the Hashira Training (2024). It is directed by Haruo Sotozaki, produced by Ufotable, and written by the studio's staff members. It follows the Demon Slayer Corps in their decisive climactic battle against Muzan Kibutsuji and the remaining Upper Ranks within the titular "Infinity Castle". Unlike the Swordsmith Village and Hashira Training adaptations, which are compilations of episodes from the anime series, Infinity Castle is a feature-length multi-film adaptation due to the arc's content and dramatic pacing, similarly to Mugen Train. It is the first film of a trilogy announced in June 2024, immediately following the airing of the fourth season's finale. It was released in Japan on July 18, 2025, by Aniplex and Toho. It was released by Crunchyroll through Sony Pictures Releasing in select Asian countries in August, before releasing in all other territories the following month. The film became the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2025, grossing $793 million worldwide, and broke numerous box office records. The film received positive reviews from critics, who praised its action sequences, visuals, and engaging story, although the pacing received some criticism. The film won numerous awards including Best Animation Film at the 49th Japan Academy Film Prize, and a record-breaking seven awards including Film of the Year at the 10th Crunchyroll Anime Awards.

messages.content:
The film became the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2025, grossing $793 million worldwide, and broke numerous box office records.
On its opening day, it earned ¥1.64 billion (US$11.11 million) with 1.15 million admissions, marking the highest opening day gross in Japanese box office history.
On the second day, it grossed ¥1.84 billion (US$12.47 million) from 1.26 million admissions.
The three-day total reached ¥5.52 billion (US$37.42 million) from 3.84 million admissions, making it the biggest opening weekend of all time in Japanese cinema.
On its fourth day, a public holiday, the film earned ¥1.79 billion (US$12.13 million) from 1.32 million admissions, bringing its four-day total to ¥7.31 billion (US$49.55 million) with 5.16 million tickets sold, making it the second-highest-grossing film of 2025 in Japan behind Detective Conan: One-eyed Flashback.
In 10 days, Infinity Castle grossed ¥2.87 billion ($87 million).
As of July 2026, the film has grossed ¥40.24 billion in Japan.
The film became the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2025, grossing $793 million worldwide, and the highest-grossing international film in the U.S.
The film grossed $70 million in its U.S.
opening weekend, setting the record for the biggest opening weekend for an international film in the U.S.
The film also broke multiple box-office records, including becoming the highest-grossing Japanese film, the highest-grossing R-rated animated film, the second-highest-grossing adult animated film and the first R-rated non-American and animated film to gross over $700 million mark, as well as overtaking The Simpsons Movie (2007) as the highest-grossing film based on an animated television series and the second highest-grossing traditionally animated film, behind The Lion King (1994).
It's also the highest-grossing traditionally animated film in its initial release, surpassing the initial gross of The Lion King.
